problem:
A metal ball of mass $0.5\,\text{kg}$ is released from rest and falls vertically downward. Let $v(t)$ be the ball's velocity, in meters per second, $t\ge 0$ seconds after release, with downward taken as the positive direction.
The air resistance on the ball is proportional to the square of its velocity with a constant of proportionality $k=0.784\,\text{kg/m}$ and acts in the direction opposite to motion.

Find the equation for the velocity $v(t).$ Assume the acceleration due to gravity is $g=9.8\,{\text{m/s}}^{2},$ and the only forces acting on the ball are the weight due to gravity and drag.

feedback.problem:
A body of mass $50\,\text{kg}$ is released from rest and falls vertically downward. Let $v(t)$ be the body's velocity, in meters per second, $t\ge 0$ seconds after release, with downward taken as the positive direction.
The air resistance on the body is proportional to the square of its velocity with a constant of proportionality $k=4.9\,\text{kg/m}$ and acts in the direction opposite to motion.

Find the equation for the velocity $v(t).$ Assume the acceleration due to gravity is $g=9.8\,{\text{m/s}}^{2},$ and the only forces acting on the body are the weight due to gravity and drag.
feedback.worked_solution:
First, note that only two forces act on the body: the force due to gravity, given by the weight

$$
w=mg=50g,
$$

and the force due to drag $D,$ which is proportional to the velocity squared (and negative since it acts in the negative direction):

$$
D=-k{v}^{2}=-4.9{v}^{2}
$$

Hence, the resultant force acting on the body is

$$
F=w+D=50g-4.9{v}^{2}.
$$

Applying Newton's second law, we obtain a separable first-order differential equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =ma \\ 50g-4.9{v}^{2} & =50\cdot \frac{dv}{dt} \\ \frac{dv}{dt} & =g-0.098{v}^{2} \\  & =g-0.01g{v}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dv}{dt} & =g(1-0.01{v}^{2}) \\ \frac{1}{1-0.01{v}^{2}}\cdot \frac{dv}{dt} & =g \\ \int \frac{1}{1-0.01{v}^{2}}\cdot \frac{dv}{dt}\,dt & =g\int dt \\ \int \frac{1}{1-(0.1v)^{2}}\,dv & =g\int dt \\ \frac{1}{0.1}\operatorname{artanh}⁡(0.1v) & =gt+{C}_{1} \\ \operatorname{artanh}⁡(0.1v) & =\frac{1}{10}gt+C \\ 0.1v & =\operatorname{tanh}⁡(\frac{1}{10}gt+C) \\ v(t) & =10\operatorname{tanh}⁡(\frac{1}{10}gt+C),\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=0.1{C}_{1}$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that the body is released from rest. So, we can apply the initial condition $v(0)=0,$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(0) & =10\operatorname{tanh}⁡(\frac{1}{10}g\cdot 0+C) \\ 0 & =10\operatorname{tanh}⁡(C) \\ \operatorname{tanh}⁡(C) & =0 \\ C & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following expression for $v(t):$

$$
v(t)=10\operatorname{tanh}⁡(\frac{1}{10}gt)
$$
